scenes.title: DynamoDB
scenes.text: On Prime Day 2025, Amazon's own systems sent one database more than a hundred and fifty million requests per second. Most of them were answered in a few milliseconds. That database is DynamoDB. Let me walk you through how it pulls that off, and when you should, and shouldn't, use it.

scenes.title: What is DynamoDB?
scenes.text: First, what is it? DynamoDB is a database that Amazon Web Services runs for you. You never set up servers, install software, or apply patches. You just create a table and start saving data. It's a NoSQL database. That means it gives up things a traditional SQL database has, like fixed columns and joining tables together. In exchange, it's built around one simple idea: find any piece of data instantly, using its key.

scenes.title: How the data is shaped
scenes.text: Here's how the data is shaped. Data lives in tables. A table holds items, and each item is a bundle of attributes, a bit like a row in a spreadsheet. The difference is that items don't need matching columns. One customer might have a phone number. Another might have a list of addresses. DynamoDB only insists on one thing: every item needs a primary key.

scenes.title: The primary key
scenes.text: That key is the most important choice you'll make, so let's look closer. It has up to two parts. The partition key decides where an item is stored. The sort key is optional, and it orders items that share the same partition key. Say we have an Orders table. The partition key is the customer ID, and the sort key is the order date. Now all of one customer's orders sit together, already sorted by date.

scenes.title: Partitions and hashing
scenes.text: So why does the partition key matter so much? Because it's how DynamoDB stays fast. A table isn't stored in one place. It's split into chunks called partitions, spread across many storage servers. When you save an item, DynamoDB runs its partition key through a hash function. That's just math that turns the key into a number, and the number points to exactly one partition. To read the item back, it does the same math and goes straight to the right place. No searching through the whole table.

scenes.title: How it scales
scenes.text: And this is the trick that lets it scale. When a partition fills up or gets too busy, DynamoDB splits it in two, and spreads the halves across more servers. Each partition only handles its own slice of the data. So a table with a billion items answers about as fast as one with a thousand. No single machine ever has to do all the work.

scenes.title: Keeping data safe
scenes.text: But servers fail all the time, so how is your data safe? Every partition is copied three times, into three separate data centers called availability zones. One copy is the leader. A write counts as saved once two of the three copies have it. If one copy goes down, the other two keep serving traffic while DynamoDB builds a replacement.

scenes.title: Two kinds of reads
scenes.text: Those copies give you a choice when you read. An eventually consistent read can be answered by any copy. It might be a split second behind, but it costs half as much. A strongly consistent read always goes to the leader, so you're guaranteed the latest data. Most apps are fine with the cheaper one.

scenes.title: Ways to read data
scenes.text: Now here's the catch. Because everything is organized by key, how you read matters a lot. Get Item fetches one item by its full key. That's the fastest. Query grabs items that share one partition key, like one customer's orders from March. Scan reads every item in the table. It works, but on a big table it's slow and expensive. If you need to look things up another way, like by order status, you add a global secondary index. That's a second copy of your data, organized by a different key, and DynamoDB keeps it in sync for you.

scenes.title: The most common mistake
scenes.text: This leads to the most common mistake. Say you pick a partition key with only a few possible values, like today's date. Then every new item lands on the same partition, while the others sit idle. That's called a hot partition, and it slows everything down. The fix is to pick keys with lots of different values, like user IDs, so the load spreads out evenly.

scenes.title: How you pay
scenes.text: A quick word on cost. You pay in one of two ways. On-demand mode charges for each request, which is great when traffic is unpredictable. Provisioned mode lets you reserve a set number of reads and writes per second, which is cheaper when traffic is steady. Storage is billed separately, by the gigabyte.

scenes.title: Strengths and weaknesses
scenes.text: So let's sum up the trade. The strengths: it's fast at any size, there are no servers to manage, it survives failures on its own, and you can pay only for what you use. The weaknesses all come from that same design. You have to know your questions up front, because your data is organized around your keys. There are no joins. And changing how you read later can mean reshaping all your data.

scenes.title: When to use it
scenes.text: So when should you use it? Reach for DynamoDB when you know ahead of time how your app will look up data, and you need it fast at any size. Think shopping carts, user profiles, game leaderboards, and login sessions. Each of those is fetched by one simple key. Skip it when you need complex joins, or want to ask new questions you didn't plan for, like one-off reports. A relational database or a data warehouse handles those better.

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.text: Here's the whole picture. Tables hold items, and every item has a key. The partition key is hashed to pick a partition. Partitions split as your data grows, and each one is copied three times. So design your keys around how you'll read, and DynamoDB stays fast, from your first user to your hundred millionth.
